CHENNAI: A 13-year-old deaf boy crossing the railway tracks near his house at Mathur Colony near Tiruttani was killed by an oncoming train on Thursday morning. The boy had gone out to relieve himself in the open because there was no toilet in the government-built house his family was living in. Police sources said he may not have heard the approaching train due to a hearing impairment he had had since birth.
The deceased was identified as K Surya Prakash, a Class 8 student at the Government Middle School in Mathur Panchayat. His father, T Kalidasan, is a daily-wage worker and his mother is a homemaker. He also has an elder sister.
Speaking to TNIE, Kalidasan said the family lived in a government-built house without a toilet and had initially petitioned the government for one but had received no response. The family was left with no choice but to use vacant plots in the surrounding area to relieve themselves. “My son sometimes uses the railway tracks and sometimes other places to relieve himself. It is not just our house, several houses in this panchayat do not have toilets,” he said.
When contacted, the block development officer for Mathur Panchayat, Selvi, said toilets were generally constructed for group houses under a government scheme. “I’m not aware of how the toilets were left out in this particular case. I will look into the matter,” she said.
Police sources said Surya Prakash had gone alone to the railway tracks around 7.50 am to relieve himself and was crossing the single track when the train hit him, killing him on the spot.
The Arakkonam GRP sent the body to Tiruvallur Government Medical College Hospital for postmortem, after which his relatives took the body home, sources said. A case has been registered under Section 194 of the BNSS, and further probe is under way.

full_text:
Flooding caused by intense rainfall and extreme heat are among the leading climate-related risks facing Humboldt, according to a new assessment presented to city council.
Mitch Bauche and Christina Hopkins of Urban Systems Ltd. presented the findings of the Climate Hazard and Risk Assessment to the city's executive committee on Oct. 14. Council received the report for information.
The study examines how changing climate conditions could affect municipal infrastructure, services, finances and residents, while identifying potential actions to improve the city's resilience.
Public Works Director Peter Bergquist introduced the presentation, explaining that the assessment will help guide the city's long-term planning.
“More importantly, it helps identify practical and prioritized actions that can be incorporated into future planning, capital projects, asset management programs, and future grant funding applications,” Bergquist told the committee.
He added that the assessment provides a framework for making decisions that account for changing conditions, helping ensure that investments made today remain effective in the years ahead.
The project was supported through the Federation of Canadian Municipalities' Green Municipal Fund, positioning Humboldt to pursue additional funding for implementation.
Flooding and extreme heat among key risks
The assessment examined climate projections, potential hazards and the vulnerability of municipal assets and services. Urban Systems worked with city staff and conducted two workshops to gather information and assess potential impacts.
The process evaluated approximately 300 interactions between climate hazards and municipal assets, assigning risk ratings based on the likelihood and consequences of potential impacts.
Rainfall-related flooding received the highest number of high-risk ratings, with six identified. Extreme heat followed with three high-risk ratings. Drought, snowmelt flooding and heavy snowfall were also identified as concerns.
Bauche said the assessment provides a clearer picture of where the city may be most vulnerable.
“What we came to at that point was identifying the highest risks,” he explained, describing how the team reviewed the risk ratings to determine which hazards warranted the greatest attention.
The findings align with flooding events Humboldt has experienced in recent years, including major incidents in 2015 and 2020, as well as more recent flooding.
Extreme heat was another significant concern, particularly in terms of its potential effects on public health, comfort and access to municipal services.

The South African Weather Service (SAWS) has warned of prolonged heatwave conditions across parts of KwaZulu-Natal, the Eastern Cape and Mpumalanga, with temperatures forecast to approach or exceed 40°C in some areas on Friday and Saturday.
The heatwave is expected to persist until Saturday in parts of the Eastern Cape, Sunday in northern KZN and Monday in much of Mpumalanga.
Extremely high fire danger conditions have also been forecast across seven provinces, while isolated thunderstorms could bring some relief to parts of the central and eastern interior.
KwaZulu-Natal
KZN faces some of the most intense heat, with SAWS warning that persistently high temperatures will continue across northern parts of the province until Sunday, 18 October.
Very hot to extremely hot and uncomfortable conditions are also expected in eastern areas.
Richards Bay is forecast to reach 39°C on Friday, with temperatures potentially climbing to 41°C on Saturday.
Pietermaritzburg is expected to reach 36°C on Friday and 39°C on Saturday, while Newcastle could experience highs of 35°C and 38°C respectively.
Durban is forecast to reach 31°C on Friday before cooling to 27°C on Saturday, when light rain is possible.
SAWS has also warned of extremely high fire danger conditions in northern KZN, particularly in areas around Ladysmith, Estcourt and Hlabisa.
Isolated showers and thundershowers are possible in the extreme northwest of the province.
Eastern Cape
The Eastern Cape remains under a heatwave advisory, with persistently high temperatures expected in parts of the Chris Hani, OR Tambo and Alfred Nzo district municipalities until Saturday, 17 October.
Extremely uncomfortable and humid conditions are also forecast south of the escarpment.
Mthatha is expected to reach approximately 36°C on Friday, while Komani, formerly Queenstown, could reach 33°C.
Temperatures in Komani are forecast to climb to 35°C on Saturday, while Mthatha could remain above 30°C.
Coastal areas will experience milder conditions, with Gqeberha forecast to reach 27°C on Friday before temperatures drop to approximately 19°C on Saturday.
SAWS has also warned of extremely high fire danger conditions across western and central parts of the province, increasing the risk of veld fires.
Mpumalanga
Heatwave conditions are expected to persist across much of Mpumalanga until Monday, 19 October, excluding areas along the escarpment.
Mbombela is forecast to reach 32°C on Friday before climbing to 35°C on Saturday.
Temperatures in eMalahleni and Ermelo are expected to reach approximately 30°C and 31°C respectively on Friday.
SAWS expects warm to hot conditions across the province, with very hot weather in places in the Lowveld.
Isolated afternoon thundershowers are possible over the southwestern Highveld.
Extremely high fire danger conditions have also been forecast for southeastern parts of Mpumalanga.
Western Cape
SAWS has warned of very hot to extremely hot and uncomfortable conditions across parts of the Central and Little Karoo.
Eastern areas of the Western Cape are also under extremely high fire danger warnings.
Despite the heat inland, Cape Town is expected to remain considerably cooler, with a maximum of approximately 20°C on Friday, dropping to 18°C on Saturday.
Rain is forecast in Cape Town on Saturday, while inland areas could remain considerably warmer.
Northern Cape
Extremely high fire danger conditions are forecast across most of the Northern Cape, where hot and largely dry conditions will persist.
Upington is expected to reach approximately 37°C on Friday, while Kimberley is forecast to reach 35°C.
Temperatures in Kimberley could rise to 36°C on Saturday, with showers and thunderstorms possible later in the day.
Springbok and De Aar are forecast to reach around 33°C on Friday.
SAWS has warned that dry conditions and high temperatures will increase the risk of rapidly spreading veld fires.
Limpopo
Hot to very hot conditions are expected across Limpopo, with extremely high fire danger warnings in northern and western areas.
Musina is forecast to reach approximately 36°C on Friday, while Thohoyandou could reach 34°C and Polokwane 31°C.
Polokwane is expected to warm slightly to 32°C on Saturday.
The province will generally experience fine conditions, although isolated afternoon thunderstorms are possible in southwestern areas on Friday.
Free State
The Free State will experience hot conditions, with SAWS warning of extremely high fire danger in western parts of the province.
Bloemfontein is expected to reach 32°C on Friday before climbing to 35°C on Saturday.
Kroonstad could reach approximately 34°C on Friday, while Bethlehem is forecast to reach 31°C.
Isolated afternoon showers and thunderstorms are possible in the extreme east on Friday, with unsettled conditions developing over parts of the province during the weekend.
North West
The North West will remain hot through the weekend, with temperatures forecast to climb into the mid-30s.
Mahikeng is expected to reach 34°C on Friday and 35°C on Saturday.
Rustenburg, Potchefstroom and Klerksdorp are all forecast to reach approximately 33°C on Friday.
SAWS expects fine and hot weather on Friday, becoming partly cloudy, with isolated afternoon showers and thunderstorms possible in the extreme east.
Gauteng
Gauteng is expected to experience warm to hot conditions, with isolated showers and thunderstorms providing some relief from the heat.
Johannesburg is forecast to reach 30°C on Friday and 32°C on Saturday.
Pretoria could reach approximately 31°C on Friday.
SAWS expects partly cloudy conditions on Friday, with isolated showers and thundershowers across the province.
The ultraviolet radiation index is expected to be high, increasing the risk of sunburn during prolonged outdoor exposure.
Public warned to take precautions
SAWS has urged residents in areas affected by extreme heat to take precautions against prolonged exposure to high temperatures.
People are advised to drink sufficient water, avoid strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest part of the day and limit exposure to direct sunlight.
Children, older people and those with existing medical conditions are particularly vulnerable to dehydration and heat-related illnesses.
Residents in areas experiencing extremely high fire danger conditions have also been urged to avoid activities that could ignite veld fires.
The weather service advised the public to monitor updated forecasts and warnings as the heatwave continues through the weekend.

DPS to Conduct Test of Orange Alert System on Wednesday, Oct. 21
The Department of Public Safety (DPS) will conduct a test of the Orange Alert Notification System on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 12:50 p.m. Please note: this is just a TEST. It will be a full test of the system, which includes notifications sent via email, text message and voice call. The test will also include the Orange Alert outdoor siren system on the University’s North and South campuses. The sirens will be activated for two minutes at 12:50 p.m.
In addition to email, text and voice messages, the Orange Alert test message will also be sent via push notification to the Orange Safe app, to the main Syracuse University and DPS Facebook and Twitter accounts, and will display on the University’s homepage and video monitors located in common areas in several buildings around campus.
Beginning this fall, our emergency notification system will include a new “desktop notifier” feature that displays emergency alerts on classroom computers and temporarily takes over the screen. Alerts will automatically close after 60 seconds, or faculty can dismiss them sooner by selecting “Acknowledge and Close” and then confirming with “Yes.”
In previous tests, notifications were typically scheduled during class transitions. With this new feature, however, the test will be conducted five minutes after classes begin.
The Orange Alert test message will be sent to all Syracuse University students, faculty and staff, SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry (SUNY ESF) students and to SUNY ESF faculty and staff who have signed up. Orange Alert will send a test notice to all devices that are registered on the system.
“Testing the Orange Alert system ensures that our campus community can be alerted quickly and effectively in the event of an emergency,” says William Karnadi, director of emergency management and business continuity planning. “This year’s test also includes a desktop notifier for the first time, so we encourage faculty and staff to expect a brief pop-up during the test window—it will be clearly marked as a test and will not disrupt your work for more than a moment. We also encourage everyone to take a few minutes to double-check their contact information in MySlice so they don’t miss these critical alerts.”
To review and/or modify your Orange Alert contact information, log into MySlice using your NetID and password, select Student Home or Employee Home, depending on your primary affiliation with Syracuse University, select the Personal Profile tile, then “Orange Alert Contacts” from the navigation menu and review your information. If you need to add, update or delete contact information, select the “Add/Update/Delete Contact Details” link. If you are a SUNY ESF student, use the SUNY ESF emergency contact information page to update your information.
For additional information on the Orange Alert system, visit the DPS website.
